question: Should the receiver be able to tell if someone changed your message?
example: You send “Send $10,” but someone changes it to “Send $100” before it arrives. Should the receiver be able to notice that the message was changed?

question: Does the receiver need to check if your message was sent recently?
example: You send a door-unlock command that should only be accepted for 30 seconds. Should the receiver check when it was sent and reject it if it is too old?

question: Does your application need to encrypt different parts of a file at the same time?
example: Encrypting means locking data so that only someone with the secret key can read it. Imagine a large file split into smaller parts. Some methods can lock several parts at once instead of one at a time. Does your application need this ability?

question: Does your application have a limit on the extra space used to store each encrypted message?
example: An encrypted message may need extra information, such as a tag that helps detect changes. This takes up storage space. Does your application have a strict limit on that extra space?

question: Does your application need to start encrypting before it knows the full message size?
example: Your application receives data a little at a time and does not yet know how much will arrive. Does it need to start encrypting before all the data arrives?

question: Would you like one method that both locks your message and checks if someone changed it?
example: Think of sending a locked box with a seal. You want one method to lock the box and help the receiver notice if someone changed what was sent. Would you prefer one method that handles both jobs?

question: If you do not need to check when a message was sent, would you prefer to skip that step?
example: Your application does not care when a message was sent. Adding a timestamp means storing and checking the time too. Would you prefer to leave out that extra step?
